## Further Reading

Bradbard, D. A., Alvis, C., & Morris, R. (2014). Spreadsheet usage by management accountants: An exploratory study. *Journal of Accounting Education*, *32*(4), 24–30. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaccedu.2014.09.001> This exploratory study asks which spreadsheet features management accountants use and which features employers expect new hires to use. It is a useful guide to the Excel skills that matter in managerial accounting work, as the role shifts from recording transactions toward decision support, planning, and control.

Caulkins, J. P., Morrison, E. L., & Weidemann, T. (2007). Spreadsheet errors and decision making. *Journal of Organizational and End User Computing*, *19*(3), 1–23. <https://doi.org/10.4018/joeuc.2007070101> Based on interviews with 45 executives, managers, and analysts in the private, public, and non-profit sectors, this paper describes how spreadsheet errors reach decisions in practice. Almost all interviewees considered errors common, and quality control was usually informal. The paper is a readable account of why the review and documentation practices in this chapter matter.

Church, K. S., Riley, J., & Schmidt, P. J. (2021). Has Excel become a "golden hammer": The paradox of data analytics in SME clusters. *Journal of Emerging Technologies in Accounting*, *19*(2), 211–234. <https://doi.org/10.2308/jeta-2020-051> This survey of small and medium-sized entities finds that they continue to perform their leading accounting tasks in Excel and lag larger firms in adopting data analytics technology. It explains why Excel skills remain central for accountants who will work in the many organizations of that size.

Panko, R. R. (1998). What we know about spreadsheet errors. *Journal of Organizational and End User Computing*, *10*(2), 15–21. <https://doi.org/10.4018/joeuc.1998040102> This widely cited synthesis concludes that errors occur in a few percent of spreadsheet cells, so that large spreadsheets almost certainly contain some. It also argues that careful inspection of a finished spreadsheet, cell by cell, may do more to catch errors than design rules alone, a useful counterweight to any claim that good structure makes a workbook correct.

Powell, S. G., Baker, K. R., & Lawson, B. (2008). A critical review of the literature on spreadsheet errors. *Decision Support Systems*, *46*(1), 128–138. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dss.2008.06.001> This review summarizes and critiques the research on spreadsheet errors from the viewpoint of a manager who wants to improve spreadsheet quality. It notes that, although errors are widely accepted to be common and costly, relatively little is known about what types of errors occur, how they arise, and how they can be avoided, and it suggests directions for further research.

Schneider, K. N., Becker, L. L., & Berg, G. G. (2017). Beyond the mechanics of spreadsheets: Using design instruction to address spreadsheet errors. *Accounting Education*, *26*(2), 127–143. <https://doi.org/10.1080/09639284.2016.1274912> Written for accounting educators, this paper argues that accounting graduates need spreadsheet design skills, not just spreadsheet mechanics. It outlines a three-step approach to teaching design practices and summarizes foundational readings on spreadsheet errors, which makes it a good starting point for further study.

Zeller, T. L., Dingrando, E., & Booker, D. (2024). Workbook design and controls: A framework. *Journal of Accounting Education*, *69*, Article 100933. <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaccedu.2024.100933> This teaching case, built from a real-world workbook, presents a framework for designing a workbook that supports a business decision: one that can be used repeatedly, reviewed by a manager, structured to minimize errors, and used interactively. It extends the organization and documentation practices of this chapter to a complete decision workbook.
